When does the minister expect to have the reports of the board of grain commissioners and the wheat board before the committee on agriculture and colonization?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: ALLEGED REDUCTION IN HOUSING STARTS THIS YEAR
speechtext:
Since the hon. member has asked that question, perhaps I should make a brief statement about housing, particularly having in mind the telegrams I have received recently which have alleged particularly two points about the house building program: first, that it is being seriously retarded because of the unavailability of mortgage money; and, second, that as a result large scale unemployment will develop. I think I can demonstrate to hon. members that both these statements reflect undue pessimism.
In centres of 5,000 population and over, as I indicated to hon. members on June 13, housing starts for the first five months of the
5328	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry year 1956 exceeded starts during the first five months of the year 1955. Up to the end of May this year, 30,687 units had been started, as against 29,669 last year. Completions at 35,322 exceeded those of the same period last year, which numbered 33,064.
As of the end of May this year there were in these centres 48,206 housing units under construction. Last year at the same time the number was 47,445. Hon. members will recall that in the year 1955 more houses were started and more were completed than in any previous year in our history.
I refer to centres of 5,000 population and over because it is in these centres that the dominion bureau of statistics and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation make complete enumerations.
As for the suggestion that significant unemployment will follow any likely downturn in housing, I would refer to the recent survey by the Department of Labour of labour conditions in Canada. At the present time there are more people employed than ever before, and fewer people without jobs. These statements have reference to the over-all labour force. The situation is that the construction industry is experiencing a shortage of manpower, and we are only now coming into the period when the demand for labour is at its peak. Thus anyone who might be laid off from house building would be apt without difficulty to find employment in other parts of the construction industry, where activity is at a record level.
While I believe that the complaints give an erroneous impression, I realize that difficulties are being experienced by some builders in obtaining mortgage funds. My colleague, the Minister of Finance, is in a good position to tell hon. members that the economy as a whole is moving at such a vigorous pace that there is keen competition for material, labour and financing. Some builders in the house building industry are feeling this competition, and particularly is this true in respect of those who have just recently come into the field. In no industry is it possible for everybody to obtain all the credit desired at all times. Government guaranteed loans under the N.H.A. are not available as of right to everybody who asks for them. It is a matter of the banks and lending institutions awarding credit on the same selective basis as applies for other industrial and commercial activities.
In the first quarter of 1956 expenditures on non-residential construction were 27 per cent higher than in the first quarter of 1955. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a supply motion it is particularly appropriate at this time that I should refer to the discussions that have already taken place here and their effect upon our present position in this house. I think it is the correct time to express our belief that this government has lost any moral right to govern this country. I know that this statement has been made, but I intend to emphasize, by reference to further material, the extent to which that moral breakdown has gone and the extent to which precedent has been abandoned.
We all know how precedents were broken in this house in a debate which took place not long ago. There was some discussion on Friday last about whether or not the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had used the words in a television interview, "We violated the rules". There is no question that those words were used. I do not think, however, that the use of those words is so particularly open to criticism. In fact, it is

the frankest statement that has been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce since this debate began. What is surprising is not that he made the statement but rather that there should be any question about the fact that he made the statement. What is important is not that the record available from the C.B.C. showed that he made the statement; what is important is the denial of the statement. The denial of the statement is consistent with the attitude of this government towards parliament.
It would have been quite natural, and quite a reasonable thing, for the minister to have said, "Well in an interview of that kind, without a text, it is easy for a person to use words which afterwards should be corrected. It is true that I did say he violated the rules, but I did not intend to say that." Nevertheless, I would think that in most interviews mistakes of that kind might be made if that was not what he intended to say. Now, if the minister had said that, that would have been a perfectly reasonable explanation. What is important is the attitude of the minister in regard to that statement. He has set himself up as the infallible director of the business affairs of this house. He has, in fact, set himself up as a virtual dictator. He is not prepared to admit that even in error he correctly stated the facts, and therefore he must repudiate what it is quite clear he said.
I am not going to say more except to repeat that the important thing is not that he did say the words; the important thing is that having said them he denied to this house that he did. It is only in keeping with many of the things that have happened. But I want to speak particularly of what has happened, not only to the House of Commons during those tragic weeks, but also what has happened to that other place which is also part of our parliamentary system. What a change has occurred from the original concept of the other place. How little it resembles in its function the purpose it was intended to serve by those who decided at Quebec when they were drafting the resolutions which were embodied in the British North America Act that we should have a second parliamentary body appointed and not elected. A high purpose was envisaged for that other place.
The fathers of confederation who met at Quebec in 1864 had an overwhelming feeling in favour of a second chamber. The possibility of a single chamber parliament was considered but, with the background of our own history, a considerable majority of those who attended that conference decided that they wanted the two-chamber system. They
25, 1956	5331
Request for Election and Senate Reform had, of course, the experience of a second chamber under two systems in this country. Under the old constitution of the united provinces there was a legislative council appointed by the crown. Then, there were the reforms of 1856 and the upper house of the legislature was made elective. Its members were chosen by direct suffrage of the people. They were entitled to serve for a term of eight years instead of a four-year term set for the members of the assembly, which was the lower house. The conditions of the franchise were the same for both houses. However, the members of the upper house represented much larger constituencies, as their numbers were smaller. At that time, strangely enough, when we had adopted an elective system, the constitution of the United States provided for the appointment of senators by state legislatures. Two were appointed from each state. That was not changed in the United States until the seventeenth amendment was adopted in 1913 to provide for the popular election of the senators to the upper body.
The system in the United States was the very opposite to what we had prior to confederation following the reforms I have spoken of. With those two systems before them the men who had seen both systems in operation decided they wanted an appointed body. In that they were undoubtedly influenced very greatly by the similarity of our parliamentary system to that at Westminster where the second and upper house, the House of Lords, was of course an appointed body. That has remained unchanged to the present day.
We have the reports of the opinions expressed by the men who made this important decision prior to confederation. The Senate, in the minds of the framers of confederation, was to consist not of partisans but of men who would deal in a judicial manner with the problems before them. Its members were to be selected from those who in one way or another had brought dignity or distinction to the public life of the country. They were to be chosen by the representatives of the sovereign for their acknowledged achievements or for their moral and intellectual excellence. They were to be placed in this position which was to keep them above the ordinary influences of party strife. It was thought at that time by the men who drafted our constitution that this would invest the members of the upper house with a moral authority which would make their decisions more acceptable when they became a body of review to consider what had taken place in the House of Commons. It was thought that the appointment in this way would detach

Request for Election and Senate Reform them from those considerations which might affect their judgment in any way from a partisan point of view.
In order to better secure the impartiality and independence of those appointed, the appointees were to be appointed for life and not for a term of years so that nothing might influence the independence of their expression of opinion and their judgment. Such an upper house would in the first place exercise immense influence upon public opinion. That was the dream of those who drafted the constitution. It was also thought that they would exercise influence on any rash decisions made by the lower house under the pressure of urgent demand or partisan debate. In every discussion the power of the upper house to review the decisions of the lower house and the likelihood and certainty that they would give careful review to the decisions of the lower house was constantly in mind.
These people who were to be appointed to the upper house and were to occupy this position of dignity and independence were to have a freedom from any influence that might spring from their dependence on re-election. Never were high expectations of that kind more completely broken and shattered than they were within these past weeks.
Reform of the upper house has been demanded for generations. Every other parliamentary body or legislative body of importance in the world has carried out sweeping reforms of its upper house in the time that ours has been in existence. It is only in the upper house of Canada that we go on without any attempt to bring the upper house into harmony with the aspirations of the people in this modern and vital democracy of ours. Nevertheless, it is not in recent years alone that the demand for reform has been emphatic and urgent. For reasons which perhaps are perfectly natural, it was the Liberal party which first began to present demands for reform of the upper house. We find that Sir Oliver Mowat, a great and distinguished member of the Liberal party of those days, presented this resolution to the Liberal party convention in Ottawa as far back as 1893. Most hon. members of this house had not yet been born at that time. This is the resolution that was adopted:
The present constitution of the Senate is inconsistent with the federal principle in our system of government and is in other respects ineffective as it makes the Senate independent of the people and uncontrolled by the public opinion of the country and should be so amended as to bring it into harmony with the principles of popular government.
Then again at the same convention, and speaking to this resolution, we find these words spoken by another very distinguished

member of the Liberal party, Sir Richard Cartwright. These were his words:
I think, sir, we all agree that the constitution of the Senate as it at present exists is a blot upon popular government and free institutions.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if those words had any meaning whatever in 1893 they certainly have meaning today because the upper house as it at present exists is precisely the same as the upper house was at that time except for the people who constitute the membership of that second chamber.
I am dealing with this subject at greater length today because I raised it briefly on Friday last and urged the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) before he left for the prime ministers' conference to initiate in consultation with the provinces a proper inquiry which would lead to a reform of the second chamber in keeping with the aspirations of our people for a democratic structure which has been brought into consonance with the development of industrial, economic, social and other conditions in this country. The Prime Minister made no response one way or the other to that request. Unfortunately, that is all too often the way in which proposals are dealt with when they are presented to this government. I am mentioning that now to point out that, when I raise this today, it might not have been necessary to go into some of the detailed remarks which I shall make had the Prime Minister acceded to what seems to be a perfectly reasonable request.
May I say at the outset, in pressing our demand for consideration of this subject, that I am not for a moment suggesting that the unfortunate features of our upper house, in so far as its composition is concerned, are not something in which both the major parties in this country have shared some responsibility over the years that have passed. The time is long overdue, however, for the implementation of the promises made by this government-and they were made by this government-to consider Senate reform and to take up with the provinces, in a manner which would lead to some positive results, this extremely important question.
On only one occasion has this matter been brought up in a comprehensive manner before a conference at which the federal and provincial governments were represented, and that was at the conference of 1927. At that time Mr. Lapointe, who was minister of justice, laid before the conference a summary of proposals which had been made by different people for Senate reform. He did so without any suggestion that he sought approval of any particular type of reform. However, these were the points he put before the conference for consideration, as reported in what

was described as "A Survey of Dominion-Provincial Conference, 1906 to 1941", by Darrell Thomas Braidwood. I quote this from page 32 of the survey:
1. Abolition of the Senate,
2. Adoption of the elective principle,
3.	A combination of both the appointive and elective principles,
4.	A fixed and limited term of office,
5.	An age limit with possible superannuation,
6.	A bringing of relations between the Canadian upper and lower chambers into accord with the relations between the House of Commons and the House of Lords in Great Britain-with particular reference to the powers of the upper house in vetoing or amending money or general public bills.
That quotation indicated the breadth of the subject matter placed before the conference. Each of these proposals was discussed but it was not followed through, and no results flowed from that discussion, nor was there any resumed examination of the proposals.
I point out that this summary made by Mr. Lapointe in 1927 did review most of the proposals which have been made for the reform of the upper house. Since then still further proposals have been made. It seems to me that it would be neither desirable nor in keeping with the purpose of the upper house to lay down an arbitrary formula which must from necessity be followed if there is to be reform. I say that because our upper house in this country had a dual purpose. Its first purpose was, of course, the ordinary review responsibility of an upper house, which corresponds to that of other upper houses under a similar parliamentary system. The second, and in many ways the most important from the point of view of those who were discussing the possibility of confederation, was that an upper house in Canada would protect the constitutional rights of the provinces under the constitution which they were about to adopt.
I think it is quite certain that there would not have been anything in the nature of the confederation that we know unless there had been an upper house to assure the protection that it was intended to give to the provinces joining in confederation. The maritime provinces were urgent and emphatic in their demand that there be an upper house which would protect their rights. The province of Quebec wanted an upper house to assure the protection of its constitutional rights, no matter what might happen at any time in the House of Commons. Ontario as well looked to the upper house to protect its own traditional rights. All the provinces looked to the upper house as the guardian of their heritage, which they were preserving under their provincial legislatures but placing in substantial measure in the keeping of the federal parliament.

The Senate adjourned at 11.45 a.m. Thus we find that this measure was dealt with in a matter of about ten hours. It is little wonder that about two days later an editorial appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail headed "Sic Transit.."Sic transit gloria" is indeed an appropriate expression. Such glory, such tradition as remained, had indeed departed on that occasion. What had happened then was not merely the incredible expedition with which the Senate had moved under this unique form of closure. It was the fact that a minister of the crown, who sits as a member of the government, had placed the upper house in a condition of subservience to the government. I think it is appropriate that I should read what was written about this event, not for the purpose of taking issue with what took place there but so that we may know what the impact of this event has been on the minds of the people of Canada.
After all, at a time when we are considering ways in which democracy must be strengthened, it is vitally important that we should not ignore representative opinion which may be taken as indicating the attitude of a substantial part of the public to any function of this parliament of ours. On June 8, the day after this matter had been disposed of, I find that the Toronto Star had an editorial under the heading, "What Purpose Does it Serve?" The opening paragraph reads as follows:
The Senate is being criticized for taking only ten hours to consider the controversial pipe line bill. Ten hours admittedly did not permit anything but the most cursory examination of the bill.
Then I would read the closing paragraph of that editorial:
If, for the reason cited, the Senate cannot take more than a superficial glance at legislation as important as the pipe line bill, what real purpose does it serve? The answer is little if any.
I am not seeking to identify myself, Mr. Speaker, with the opinion of one newspaper or another in regard to the statements that they may make. I am simply seeking to indicate to hon. members of this house what has happened with respect to the attitude of newspapers in Canada towards a part of the bicameral system under which we take our

responsibilities as members of parliament. In the Toronto Telegram for June 7, the same day as that adjournment took place, there was an editorial under the heading, "The Impotent Senate". I read the first sentence in that editorial:
A meek and obedient Senate has suspended its rules and passed the government's pipe line measure in undignified and subservient haste.
Then I refer to the editorial in the Globe and Mail on June 9 to which I have already referred under the heading "Sic Transit..
I shall read two paragraphs from that editorial:
The Senate is supposed to be detached from the hurly-burly of political seeking and striving. In that detachment, it is supposed to look calmly, carefully at legislation sent on to it by the Commons; having power, if it wishes, to amend that legislation or to reject it completely. The Senate did not reject the sinister pipe line bill, nor amend it by one iota. It did not even take the time to have a good look at it, but rushed the bill through in a day and a half, so as to meet the deadline imposed on it.
Then I read the last paragraph of that editorial:
Sic transit gloria. Perhaps it is true, as some say, that the Senate no longer serves any useful function in Canadian life. Perhaps it does not even provide, as some say, security for deserving politicians in their old age. The Senate conducted itself this week as though it were anything but secure; as though, like the government majority in the House of Commons, it could only survive by licking the boots of its master.
Mr. Speaker, I wish just to read an editorial which appeared in the Calgary Herald, a newspaper which has been regarded as being very independent in the expression of its opinions. That newspaper is also situated in a province where there was reason for some particular interest in this issue. I should like to read that editorial because, even in that province where there could be many reasons for perhaps looking with more favour than elsewhere on some of the steps that were taken to expedite proceedings, we find this reflection of the impact on public opinion of what took place in the upper house at the bidding of one of the members of this government. The heading of that editorial is "How did the Senate serve Canada?" and it reads as follows:
The pipe line deal is now the law of the land.
It became law right on schedule, June 7.
The schedule was maintained in the House of Commons by use of a battering-ram operated by the Rt. Hon. C. D. Howe, and Prime Minister St. Laurent.
And it was speeded on its way to royal assent by a pusillanimous performance by the Senate of Canada.
It is of this last phase that we propose to speak.
The House of Commons has to its credit, at least, the fact that a valiant fight was put up, a fight to
Request for Election and Senate Reform the finish for the traditional rights of parliament and for the good of the Canadian people.
The Senate has nothing whatsoever to its credit.
This vaunted Other Place of sober second thought, this guardian against tyranny and improvidence, this citadel of life-appointment independence, what did it do? It submitted to a gag to which it did not have to submit. Then it went tiredly through a few motions, as though it were really alive. And then, in unashamed subservience to its Liberal masters, it doffed its cap and did the government's bidding voluntarily, right on schedule.
We say these things in bitter sorrow, for on repeated occasions we have come to the defence of the Senate as a valuable institution when others, many others, were baying for its abolition. And if the Senate of Canada conducted itself as tradition demands, we would gladly defend it again. The loss of a proper Senate would be a sore blow, a dangerous blow, to our system of parliamentary democracy. The loss of a Senate which bowed and scraped as this one did this week would be no loss at all. It is a mockery, a sham, an expensive luxury, far too expensive to keep around for minor chores like granting divorces.
Can anybody point to one single useful thing the Senate of Canada did in this pipe line affair, the most controversial, perhaps the most significant decision this country has had to make in modern history? Can anybody point out one constructive thing it did? Did it probe, did it query, did it demand that it be satisfied that a great blunder was not being made? Did it appear to be protecting any Canadian against anything? The answer in all cases is a melancholy "No".
It is understandable that Liberals in the Commons might have been reluctant, for obvious reasons, to step out of line no matter what their private opinions.
No such practical pressures bear on any Senator. But still, with nothing to fear, unreachable by political vengeance, the Liberals in the Senate behaved like sheep.
They ought to be ashamed. Meantime, we are ashamed for them.
Mr. Speaker, that is the impact this sorrowful event had on the thinking of one of the most independent newspapers in Canada. I could read a number of other editorials from other papers as well as articles which have been written which leave no uncertainty as to the shameful destruction of respect which has taken place at the instance of a member of this government who was able to persuade the subservient members of that Senate to follow the will of the government in a new form of blanket closure which disposed of any pretence that this is any longer a serious body of sober second thought. In this house opinions differ as to the desirability of continuing the Senate. I know that, in great sincerity, there are hon. members in this house-and they are not of one party alone-who believe that the time has come when the Senate might be abolished. I do not share that opinion. I believe that it is the opinion of the majority, if not all, of the members of the party to which I belong that there are strong constitutional reasons, as well as reasons of tradition and sentiment, why the second chamber

Request for Election and Senate Reform should be preserved but in a form in which it will be permitted to perform the duties that were contemplated by those who brought it into being in 1867. Surely it is not reflecting upon any hon. member of that other place to say that the upper house needs drastic reform if their attendance there is to be justified. Let no hon. member in that other place who declares his allegiance to the Liberal party suggest that there is anything partisan in demanding that in the interests of respect for our parliamentary system there be reform. After all, who could make stronger statements on this subject than Sir Richard Cartwright who, in a very pithy sentence, said this:
I think, Sir, we all agree that the constitution of the Senate, as it at present exists, is a blot upon popular government and free institutions.
That was the other place in the same form as it now is, without reform. If those words were not too strong then, still stronger words could be used today. Perhaps no stronger words need be used than those powerful words of the Calgary Herald which were unquestionably written with the deep feeling of someone who believes in and respects our existing constitution. I share the view of whoever wrote that editorial when he speaks of the danger of losing the second chamber unless there is a change.
If things go on as they are, if this government continues in power and imposes its will on the other place as it did on this occasion, then the demand for the abolition of the other place may come to the point where it might not be possible to stem the tide of that demand. I would hope, and I do hope very strongly, that it may be possible to take steps in time to stem that tide. I think there would be very grave concern in the minds of the members of our legislative bodies throughout Canada if the supposed protection, if the intended protection, of the upper house were completely removed. I am not putting myself in the position of suggesting that on recent performance they have any reason to believe that the other place, as now constituted, does offer them any real protection. For that reason I would hope that the members of the provincial legislatures are examining with care and with great concern what has happened to the upper house.
It was bad enough when they were denied the opportunity to do an effective job; it was bad enough when a one-sided chamber made any effective second examination no longer a possibility; but now we have come to something that is no longer a question of the composition of the other place, no longer a question of the opportunity it has to deal with legislation or the procedures which


are followed, but the dignity, honour and independence of the other place have been destroyed in the same way that the dignity, the honour, and the independence of high offices in this house were destroyed at the same time. That is the serious feature. I would hope that we would hear an echoing demand from the other place. I would not wish any hon. member of the other place to think that I am reflecting on any individual. I believe that there are people of high integrity, of great experience, of long training, who could serve Canada well in that other place.
In Britain at Westminster the House of Lords, which is the corresponding second body, has been drastically reformed. A system has been established under which the House of Lords can have an effective voice, not only in regard to ordinary legislation but in regard to money bills as well under certain limiting provisions. The House of Lords cannot hold up legislation indefinitely. A recent provision makes it possible for the House of Lords to veto a measure, and then it would come back to the commons. When the House of Commons passed it a second time, it would become law. I believe that is the most recent revision. The House of Lords as an appointed body, for that reason, has a vitally important part in the functioning of parliament. It also has wider opportunities for the initiation and review of legislation, and for the consideration of many important subjects.
I believe that our second house, under our parliamentary system, could perform a most useful service. I believe there are types of legislation, other than divorce legislation, which they could handle with great expedition. They could discuss these subjects in that detached atmosphere which is supposed to prevail there, and then this legislation would be brought before this house with the advantage of the advice of experts in that field who would have been brought before the Senate committee before this house was called to pass upon it. I think an amendment of the upper house, which in no way changed its constitutional relationship to the provinces, could greatly shorten the sessions of this house and bring about a better balance between the work of the two houses than exists at this time. I hope that I will not be regarded as being unduly envious when I mention that there are many members here who wish they were members of the other place when it adjourns from time to time because there is not sufficient work before it. My comment is no reflection on the other place. There is no reason for them to continue in Ottawa when they have no work

before them. I think that what is essential for the effective operation, not only of the other place but of the House of Commons, is that under a proper system of reform, which maintains the protective feature of the other place's constitutional relationship to the provinces, there will be a balance of work between the two houses that will keep them closer together in their time tables and not cause the members of the other place to move back and forth from time to time as they are called upon to do during the course of the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question for the purpose of clarification? Would he go so far as to propose that in the division of work between the other place and the House of Commons, money bills could be initiated in the other place?

No, I am not suggesting that money bills, in general, be initiated in the other place. After all, if there is one thing that above all else does attach itself to the responsibility of the government, it is the initiation of money bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Yes, that is why I asked the question.

There is every possibility of a reference of money bills in the way that has been established in the House of Lords at Westminster. It was in regard to such a reference of money bills that I made the suggestion that we might, perhaps with some advantage, consider what had been done there. I wish to leave no uncertainty, however, because I did say this before. I am not seeking to lay down any rigid formula. The provinces have a very important part to play in whatever is done, and while there must be a keen desire to work out a balance between the work of the two houses which will give to the very distinguished and highly trained members of that upper house a wider scope for their training and experience, we must also remember that there should be no diminution of the authority of the other place over the constitutional relationship between the provincial governments and the federal government which was contemplated in the original drafting of our basic constitution. That, of course, also is inherent in the fact that the members of the upper house are not appointed on the basis of representation by population. The numbers are fixed. There is agreement as to that. The appointments are made with recognition of the unique duality of its function, of the duty of the upper house in relation to the provinces and their constitutional position, and also the relationship

I mention that because the discussion that takes place should be brought forward, as it was brought forward by the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe in 1927, before a conference representative of the federal and provincial governments. My hope would be, though, that with what has happened and with the urgent desire to revive respect for the role of the upper house and its traditions, we should carry this forward, or see it carried forward, to a satisfactory conclusion which would be acceptable to the provinces and to both houses.
I say this without in any way accepting the proposition that is sometimes put forward that when we urge a reform of the other place here in this house it would of necessity be repudiated by the other place. I cannot believe that, Mr. Speaker. I cannot believe that men and women of great ability, chosen to fill an honoured position in the upper house, would not welcome a reform which would give them an opportunity to play their full part in the operation of the parliament of Canada at this important time.
It is not only at Westminster that these reforms have taken place. In Australia they have had sweeping reforms and they elect their upper house. I have said I would hope we would not come to that point. In New Zealand, under demands such as have arisen here, they have abolished the upper house.
I hope that does not happen here. The danger, however, will increase as events of this kind occur.
Now, Mr. Speaker, today on this supply motion I have dealt with one particular subject and I intend to move an amendment which does not relate to this subject alone but which does re-emphasize our belief that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) should take those constitutional steps which would bring about a dissolution of this house and an election at the earliest possible date. We have emphasized that before. There was an interjection the other day that this was being done in a half-hearted manner. I have not heard anything half-hearted about the demands that have been made. We wish to remove any suggestion that there is anything half-hearted about our demand that there be dissolution and an election which will give the Canadian people the chance to express their opinions. We have spoken with deep earnestness, and we speak with deep earnestness today when we say that a great tragedy has occurred in the parliament of Canada, not only in this house but in the other place as well. Emphasis has been placed in this house on the tragedy to the House of Commons, on the events which placed the position of the Speaker, the chairman of the

We have spoken of the concern and the grave concern we feel for the future, with the precedents that have been established in regard to a form of closure never before at any time contemplated which, in the hands of people who sought to destroy parliament, could be applied as effectively as measures were ever employed under any dictatorship. It may be easy to say, "Oh, well, that cannot happen here". This has been said in most countries where free parliaments were destroyed by the methods and procedure of democracy itself, and that after all is the way in which it has happened in many lands.
We saw a system adopted here which denied to the house the opportunity to discuss individual measures, and yet found a declaration made that we had given consideration to sections of a bill which were never before us for a moment. No; things have happened here in rulings in this house by the Chair and by the chairman of committees which could be very dangerous precedents for the years ahead.
After the debate closed here and the votes were taken, things happened in the other place which were a part of this whole evil attempt-and I confess, a successful attempt -to bend parliament to the will of one man, to the will of a man who does not like the rules of parliament, and the will of a man who has been able to get the support of the other members of the government as well as the members of his own party for the demands he has made. Only a year ago we sat here well on into the summer because of the demands that that man made for unprecedented powers which had never been exercised in peacetime and never written into the statutes as they then proposed to do. That debate came to a successful conclusion in so far as the people of Canada were concerned because the government finally acceded to our proposals that a limit be placed upon those wide powers, and in that way the law should not become part of the permanent statute law of Canada, which would have practically made it possible for the government by order in council at any time to have dealt with any aspect of our economy. We were successful then; we were not successful on this occasion except to the extent that we did arouse a public consciousness of what was taking place here.
I am well aware, as is every hon. member, that there is a large majority on the government side. Mr. Speaker, I think the free press of Canada-and I use these words without capitals-on this occasion did indicate clearly what the people were thinking. I believe that those of us who opposed the course followed 

by the government were in fact expressing the sentiment of the people of Canada. I believe the people of Canada were shocked and ashamed at the arbitrary action taken by this government to comply with a date line set by a company which was not even controlled by people from our own country. I believe that Canadians are sickened by what has happened here in this House of Commons and in the other place.
I urged the Prime Minister to take some action such as the Prime Minister could take and such as the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe obviously contemplated a few years ago when he presented these suggestions to a conference. There was no reply just as there was no reply on the other occasion to set up a committee on defence.
Before I sit down I just want to refer to that because I did not have the opportunity to do so and it shows exactly how far this goes. When I asked that the committee on defence be set up the Prime Minister said we could not have that committee because that was a practice followed in Washington. I then informed him there were inquiries of this kind in Britain. He said that was not his understanding but he would make inquiries. I need only remind him that it is done here and it is done every year by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) when he refers his estimates to a standing committee for that department. These are merely examples of the way in which this government denies to this house the opportunities to assume its responsibilities. I do not believe there will be a full acceptance of parliamentary rights nor will there be a parliament in keeping with the wishes of the people of Canada until there has been a change.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker): That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
in the opinion of this house the Prime Minister should give immediate consideration to the advisability of bringing about the dissolution of this parliament and the calling of a general election as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker I rise to support the amendment. It is perfectly obvious to me that the present House of Commons has lost the confidence of the country.
No.

This is something that first of all grieved me and then angered me and

Request for Election and Senate Reform the thing that grieved me most in all probability was the fact that over the years I have believed that many of the hon. gentlemen sitting opposite may have believed in democratic procedures, and to see them set aside by the people in whom I had some confidence as democrats was indeed a very sorry thing to observe in this house.
My hon. friend can make his speech when I sit down.
He would not have nerve enough to.
I have no doubt that his remarks stem back to some of his background in the past-party solidarity. My hon. friend knows to what I am referring. It stems from some of his background in the past.
My background will stand up against yours any time.
He is an independent.

We take a somewhat different attitude to the other place from that expressed by the Leader of the Opposition. For many years we have seen no good purpose in continuing a second chamber which simply does the bidding of the government, and again if ever a demonstration were needed of the second chamber doing the bidding of the government it was in connection with this pipe-line matter.
When it comes to the Canadian Senate, I think we could modify a famous saying: Everybody talks about the Senate but nobody ever does anything about it. That is true of whatever party is in power in this country.
Right from the earliest days of confederation, the appointments to the Senate by Sir John A. Macdonald were being criticized by the Liberals of that day. Subsequently, when the Liberals were in power, the appointments to the Senate were criticized by the Conservatives. Today we have a Senate which is no longer representative of anything but itself and the Liberal party, a Senate which is predominantly Liberal and where the opposition members in the Senate-and I speak respectfully of them-mostly have reached an age Where the long hours of parliamentary debate and so on cannot be sustained by them. The very fact that in ten hours they were able to put through the measure that they did put through in connection with the pipe line is, I think, sufficient evidence that the Senate is no longer functioning and indeed should be abolished.
As far as reform is concerned, I believe it would be much easier to abolish the Senate chamber than to reform it. There would be

a long controversy in the country as to how it was going to be reformed, but a simple proposal placed before the people of Canada for the abolition of the Senate would, I believe, be sustained by the people of Canada.
True, we know that under the confederation agreement the Senate was supposed to protect the rights of minorities, but when at any time in recent years has the Senate protected the rights of minorities, and particularly the rights of those of the other language than the one I am using myself this afternoon? I think the answer is never. The Senate has never done anything, that I know of, to protect the rights of the French-speaking Canadians, and for a very good reason. The very good reason is that it is not needed to protect those rights. Those rights are amply protected now, first of all by the constitution of this country itself, the British North America Act; then, of course, by the courts of our country and particularly, perhaps, the Supreme Court of Canada; and then the manner in which the representation in this house is set up, guaranteeing representation as the population of the province of Quebec and the other provinces grows. Then, of course, another reason for the fact that protection is no longer needed is the growth of the French-speaking population in our country and the influence exerted by our Frenchspeaking compatriots. Today the protection of those minority rights, as they were thought of at the time of confederation, is no longer needed from a Senate of Canada.
I am of the opinion that the people of Canada would welcome a proposal for the abolition of the Senate. It is true, as I think the Leader of the Opposition indicated, that in all probability, the consent of the Senate being required, it would be very difficult to pass legislation to bring that about by a joint address, shall we say, of both houses of parliament, but I am sufficiently democratic in my point of view to think that, if the Canadian people indicated in a very clear and certain manner that they wanted either to reform the Senate or to abolish the Senate, the democratic desire of the people of a democratic country would ultimately prevail.
As I see it, there can be no logical reason today in a democracy for an appointed institution of this description. As the Leader of the Opposition has said already-and I do not want to go into details, because he has done so-the House of Lords has been very considerably curtailed in its powers. The Senate of Canada, modelled on the House of Lords, still retains all the power that the British House of Lords had. It can veto any bill, if it dares to do so, and it can exercise powers that the House of Lords

exercised once but can no longer exercise. It seems to me that, if the more, shall 1 say, traditional-minded British people can curtail the power of their second chamber in the manner in which they have done, we should be able to deal with our second chamber at least in the same manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. member mind a question?
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is it not a fact, though, that the destruction imposed in the United Kingdom on the House of Lords is with respect to their powers, and not with respect to their composition?

Yes, certainly with respect to their powers and not to their composition, but I am hoping that their composition will be changed. Let me say this to my hon. friend: that appointments to the House of Lords by all recent governments of Great Britain have not been made on a partisan basis. They have been very largely made of men of outstanding service to the country, of outstanding ability in law, in parliament, in the armed services, in education and in other places, whereas our appointments in this country have been made mainly on a partisan basis, and very often the people who have been appointed are people who tried to get elected in constituencies and could not achieve the desired result and were put into the Senate as a reward for their services to the party in power. It is predominantly now a Liberal Senate.
So I say that the hon. gentleman is quite right when he says that the constitution is different. Of course, we do not want the hereditary principle in Canada, and I think that sooner or later it will be dispensed with in the United Kingdom. I think it is worth while referring briefly to the record in this regard, Mr. Speaker. That is far from the situation. Without taking the time of the house to put it all on the record, I wish to establish this point. Section 145 of the British North America Act is the keystone of this entire structure. This is what it says:
Inasmuch as the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick have joined in a declaration that the construction of the Intercolonial Railway is essential to the consolidation of the union of British North America, and to the assent thereto of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick . . .
That is the prime condition on which they entered. It is interesting to see the technological advances that have taken place since 1867. Eight years later Prince Edward Island was brought in and virtually the same thing was said. However, they were then emphasizing telegraphs as well. We come to 1948 and Newfoundland finally comes into the dominion. The technological field has developed still further. Now we have airports, airplanes, railways, telegraph; the whole picture. As the technological field has developed so I suggest should the interpretation of this problem and what is envisaged by it.
The whole matter of the Maritime Freight Rates Act was considered many years ago, away back in 1926. It would be worth while, Mr. Speaker, if time permitted, to put on the record the preamble of the Maritime Freight Rates Act.

I did not realize there was that much, Mr. Speaker. The Maritime Freight Rates Act was passed in 1927. There was a preamble to that act which is very important, and which for some reason has been left out of the printing of the act in the Revised Statutes of Canada. In order to find the preamble one has to go back to the original statute. I think it is worth while to put on the record what was said by the royal commission as a basis for the establishment of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. It was as follows:
Whereas the royal commission on maritime claims by its report, dated September 23, 1926, has, in effect, advised that a balanced study of the events and pronouncements prior to confederation, and at its consummation, and of the lower level of rates which prevailed on the Intercolonial system prior to 1912, has in its opinion confirmed the representations submitted to the commission on behalf of the maritime provinces, namely, that the Intercolonial Railway was designed, among other things, to give to Canada in time of national and imperial need an outlet and inlet on the Atlantic ocean, and to afford-
These are the important words, Mr. Speaker:
-to maritime merchants, traders and manufacturers the larger market of the whole Canadian people instead of the restricted market of the maritimes themselves, also that strategic considerations determined a longer route than was actually necessary, and therefore that to the extent that commercial considerations were subordinated to national, imperial and strategic conditions, the cost of the railway should be borne by the dominion, and not by the traffic which might pass over the line.
There are several other sections, but this is the important one. One of the purposes of the railway was strategic, Mr. Speaker, which resulted in a railway 300 miles longer than was necessary. That is rather interesting today, Mr. Speaker, when we have our United States friends co-operating, in fact working, in the north country and taking over the D.E.W. line. One reason we in the maritime provinces are penalized in regard to freight rates is that when we entered confederation there was a real or imagined fear of the United States, and the Intercolonial Railway was built all the way up along that New Brunswick coastline, as far away as possible from the United States border. That resulted in an increased mileage of over 350 miles. Our goods have to move back and forth over these miles to get to central Canada.

Up to the early part of 1912, in fact up to the outbreak of the first world war, those rates were preserved at a proper level. The principle was maintained that the traders and manufacturers of the maritimes should get into the larger market of upper Canada. Those rates started to increase during the war. The Maritime Freight Rates Act was brought into effect in 1926. In effect they froze the rates at a certain level and gave a reduction of 20 per cent on goods originating within certain areas in the maritime provinces moving into the markets of Quebec and Ontario.
That seemed to be a satisfactory solution. Then what happened? We began to get these horizontal increases at one time and another, until recently it*was computed that from 1948 to 1955, because of horizontal increases, the freight rates had increased over 98 [DOT] 7 per cent. When we take into consideration the 7 per cent increase which was authorized the other day by the board of transport commissioners we have had an increase of over 100 per cent since 1945.
What a bill to give to a territory which used to get a 20 per cent reduction. When the principle was established one might be paying $1, and with the 20 per cent reduction it amounted to 80 cents. That put us in a competitive position. In the meantime that rate has gone up to 82 and now we are paying $1.60. It is true that we are getting the 20 per cent reduction, but we are paying $1.60 instead of the 80 cents we were paying before because those horizontal increases have not applied to traffic in Ontario and Quebec where there is competition from water transportation and from trucks. Because of these short-haul, competitive rates which have been established, goods in this part of the country have not borne the same relative costs as they have in the maritime provinces. I could produce example after example of that but I am not going to do it at the moment because the situation is well known to all of us.
Now, someone has said, "You are getting special subsidies, a special benefit." Premier Flemming said, when he mentioned the Maritime Freight Rates Act, he sometimes felt like a poor relative looking for charity. I suggest to this house that in the short time I have been here we have provided special subsidies for transportation. We provided it in connection with the railway bridge across northern Ontario. We pay $7 million a year for the reduction of rates across that northern Ontario bridge. If you take the car loadings moving you will find that the subsidy per car on the so-called bridge is $48.44. I find that reference in the study made by the

This is just illustrative of the problem which exists in my own constituency. When this act came into effect, and as late as 1937, a carload of apples going from Middleton in my constituency to Montreal cost $120 and in 1955 it cost $272. A carload of apples going from Grimsby, Ontario, to the Montreal market in 1937 cost $97 and that was increased to only $127 by 1955. In other words a carload of apples being shipped under the so-called benefits of the Maritime Freight Rates Act has had an increase of $148 imposed on it, and a carload getting standard rates from Grimsby to Montreal has had an increase of $30. So we are $118 worse off under the so-called benefits of the Maritime Freight Rates Act than under the other rates.
I can also quote figures for a carload of lumber from Ontario to New Brunswick. It was $80 in 1937 and it is $160 today, or an increase of 100 per cent. From Val d'Or Quebec to Montreal it was $86 in 1937 and it is $111 today.
One could go on, Mr. Speaker, but I think I have said enough to give some examples of the complete failure of the Maritime Freight Rates Act to operate under existing conditions. This act does not apply to shipments going to the United States. It goes back to the time of the building of the Intercolonial Railway, when the Duncan commission felt we could have nothing except what we were logically entitled to as the result of confederation. Back at the time of confederation reciprocity with the United States had just been abrogated and the maritimes were shipping very little to the markets of Massachusetts and New England. In 1926 the Duncan commission said, "You cannot get any benefit

from goods going into the United States". Today, of course, we are shipping large quantities of apples and vegetables, some lumber and tremendous quantities of fish into the New England states, and thus we should get the benefit of that act.
For some strange reason which no one has been able to determine the act has been administered so that it does not apply to goods moving by C.P.R. into Nova Scotia, coming over from Saint John to Digby. As a result goods moved over that route by the Canadian Pacific Railway into Nova Scotia are paying the highest rates in the maritimes. No change has been made so far and apparently no change is being contemplated by this government. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say the time has come when that act must be revised. It must be brought up to date and applied to give us that to which we are entitled.
We do not want that to which we are not entitled; not charity or grants in aid or assistance of any kind except the fundamental matters which were guaranteed by the British North America Act, recognized by a commission appointed by this government in 1926, and written into the preamble of the act, all of which have been lost through technological changes in transport and freight rates by two innovations:	(a) horizontal increases and
(b) by creating special rates to meet competition by water and truck. The situation today in the maritimes is much more adversely prejudiced by the act being in existence than it was 25 years ago before the act came into existence at all.
As I said, that is only the third matter I want to bring to the attention of the house at this time. It is a matter that was outstanding long before I came to the house.
