The government said it would take it under consideration and something would be done. This afternoon I was looking at the speech made by the then minister of transport, Mr. Chevrier, in which he admitted there had been difficulties in the administration of the act and said something must be done about it.
That took place in 1949, and this is 1956. Is there any reason one should not say that is a matter on which there is a justifiable complaint? We in the maritimes believe this government has failed in dealing with this problem and that it is necessary to have a new parliament elected with a fresh government to deal with this and a score of other problems which may or may not be raised during this debate.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that to some extent I have enjoyed listening to the Leader of the Opposition make his annual speech concerning why the Senate should be reformed. Listening to his address I admit I thought a logical amendment would have been to the effect that it was resolved the government should bring in a bill to reform the Senate, but the Leader of the Opposition did not bring that in. I am not championing the cause of the Senate because I want to go there. I shall be in the House of Commons for as long a time as the people of Fort William want me to be here, and while I am here I will not be in the Senate.
If I had been a senator sitting up yonder looking down on the Commons during the pipe-line debate there is one question I would have asked myself: Why does the opposition not debate the bill? Why are they moving so many motions for the adjournment of the house, and why are they raising so many points of order and questions of privilege? Why do they not debate the bill?
I will admit, Mr. Speaker, that when the pipe-line bill went to the Senate the Senate debated the bill with dignity, and in proportion to their number they said more in the discussion of the bill than did the opposition here. The opposition in the Senate did not get angry and rush out into the aisle calling the other side names and doing other undignified things. I must also confess, Mr. Speaker, that during that fracas I was the only one on this side of the house who did not act with dignity. When an hon. member over yonder called out, "Throw out the mace", and then when the leader of the C.C.F. and other hon. members came out in the aisle like a howling mob, I must say I stepped out into the aisle and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, though I might have gone down under the advance of the members, somebody else would have known the reason before I would have allowed anybody to touch the mace. I think the Senate would be well advised to send a bill down to this house for the reform of the House of Commons, after what the members of the Senate saw take place here.
The policy of the government was that we would have an all-Canadian gas pipe line for Canada. That was expressed in the speech from the throne. One hon. member who was not a Liberal said to me, "If the government does not pass this bill, if it allows the opposition to defeat it in this respect, it is not fit to govern the country". But the opposition did not win this time, and I would just like to remind the opposition that those who came out into the aisle using language they
25, 1956	5349
Request for Election and Senate Reform would never use to their better halves will regret that scene as long as they live.
Perhaps the Senate does need some reform, but I am not going to go into that now. I am going to say, however, I think the government stands high in the estimation of the people of Canada, and I am going to allow a cabinet minister to prove that.
Bring on an election if you think so.

I am not listening to any questions from the opposition when a man does not rise in his place. I was home in Fort William. If we had not passed the pipe-line bill I doubt that I could have been elected again there. Perhaps I could not be anyway. But that is the government policy. When I think of the government of Ontario to a man standing for this pipe line and then the opposition here trying to do everything possible to defeat it, I think there is another thought coming to the opposition.
As I have said, I shall allow a cabinet minister to show why the government is held in higher respect in Canada today than ever before. We have better times today than ever we had before; unemployment is low; and today we have an atmosphere in Canada that many other countries in the world would like to imitate.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Westminster):
speechtext:
The
motion of non-confidence that the leader of the official opposition moved reads:
In the opinion of this house the Prime Minister should give immediate consideration to the advisability of bringing about the dissolution of this parliament and the calling of a general election as soon as possible.
It is one in which every Canadian should be most vitally interested. I listened with some interest to what he had to say with respect to the reform of the Senate. I must say that possibly much of what he said thereto was called for, and that our upper chamber was drastically in need of some reform. I am satisfied, too, that possibly the senators themselves desire certain changes to be brought about in the operation of that august chamber. However, I do not view this amendment as one that would be a vote of confidence in the government; rather I think it would indicate that it is a vote of confidence in democracy itself.
It would seem to me that here we have many instances where a minority group feels that because it has not had its way, the government is not rightfully in office. I listened with a great deal of interest some days ago when the Leader of the Opposition spoke in respect to the vote of censure on Mr. Speaker. The only fault I heard him find,
5350	HOUSE OF
Request for Election and Senate Reform was that Mr. Speaker admitted he had made a mistake and was trying to do something about it. I for one consider that when a man makes a mistake and is big enough in a chamber such as this to admit he has made a mistake, he should be given credit and not censured for it.
In dealing with the trans-Canada pipeline bill the official opposition and the C.C.F. apparently were ill-disposed to feel that the bill was a good one for this country. They have a right to their opinions, but I wish they had said more about the bill at that time and less about the rules of procedure, and had let us discover what they had to offer in place of it. Then possibly some of us might have been more prone to support them in that particular case.
In respect to the matter of education, raised earlier by one of the members of the Conservative group, I think he indicated he felt that the federal government should do more in respect to education. I have supported from time to time a plea that the federal government should assist in education to a greater degree than it is doing today, especially in the higher grades. That would not be a mistake. However, it would be a mistake on the part of this parliament to foist its ideas upon any of the provinces that do not wish us to assist in education at the federal level, and for that reason I again feel, much as I would like to see assistance in the education field by the federal authority, that it is impossible for me to agree that it should be forced upon any group in this country that does not wish it.
The future of democracy will not be met by this bigoted action but, I should say, rather by a moral acceptance of the responsibility of each member of this house that he has a job to do here. His job in the opposition, I should say, is to try to persuade the government that what it is doing is wrong and possibly might be amended, but certainly not to tell this country that after a government has been elected by the people for an understandable period of four or five years if it so wishes, it must do as the minority says it should do or else go to the country every time there is a contentious measure.
A year ago we in this group most heartily supported the opposition in respect to the defence production bill. Even on that issue, however, unless the people of this country are stirred up to the extent that they show they are absolutely opposed to the reigning government, I feel that no election is called for and we should carry on in a practicable way and let democracy function as it is
[Mr. Hahn.l

intended to function, by the rule of the majority and not by the rule of the minority.
I think it is to our discredit that we should say that we as M.P.'s are not exercising the authority that is vested in the office we hold; that some of us are voting for a particular political machine. I am satisfied that each member of this house, including each of the hon. members on this side, when they took the oath of office agreed they would do as their conscience bade them, and I am not going to accuse anybody of not having done so. If it would appear that certain members have followed in the footsteps of their leaders and followed their suggestions, it may be that persuasion was the driving force that caused it. It is not a force of fists, but possibly a force of words and explanations that showed them the merits of what they were voting for.	.
The fact is that I find in my own area at least, for that is the area from which I get most of my correspondence, that there is no extreme discontent, and I consider that would be the prime reason for any election to be held in this country. Certainly at this time, in considering what has taken place in this country, no matter how badly we feel about the events that have taken place I cannot see sufficient reason for calling an election and so doing us out of the proper field of democracy as it is expected to function. Probably I should be the last to suggest that we should not have an election, for I am possibly one of the very few in this house who at this time have been favoured with a nomination to contest the next election. Personally I would be quite ready for it, but I see no reason for it. I am satisfied that those who are clamouring the most for it would be the most disappointed should the government call an election immediately.
Nomination does not mean election.

I take note of the interjection with respect to nomination not meaning election. There is no one more aware than I am of the fact that nomination does not mean election. I was one of the few who were declared defeated and later elected in the last election. However, it will remain for my constituents to decide, and I will be prepared to let them decide the issue in due course. But I do not consider that this is the proper time for such an election.
The question of freight rates was raised. As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings did, I should also like to indicate that I am quite opposed to the latest increase in the freight rate structure of this country. It is true that the board of transport commissioners

determined that a 7 per cent hoist in rates at the present time was quite justified, having regard to the increases in wages that were given to certain railway employees. However, freight rates play such an integral part in this nation, especially in the parts that are distant from Ottawa and the central provinces, that they have a material effect upon the cost of living; in fact to such a degree that I am satisfied the whole nation may well suffer if we continue to have increases in freight rates every time there is an increase in wages.
Agriculture in Canada has suffered badly during the past few years. We have been told by members of all parties, and the statistics bear it out, that agriculture is suffering more at the present time and also suffered more last year than at any time since the depression years. In British Columbia we have a strong agricultural industry. It is the third major industry of the province, being surpassed only by logging and mining. There are certain branches of agriculture in that province which require a great deal of wheat.
I refer to the poultry, dairying, pork and beef industries. We are not primarily a graingrowing area, so we have to import a great deal of grain into the province from our neighbours.
The increase in the price of grain brought about by the 7 per cent increase in freight rates is merely going to put our farmers into a 14 per cent cost squeeze. The farmer will have to pay 7 per cent more on domestic grain coming into his area and an additional 7 per cent on the other goods he has to purchase. The two combined add to 14 per cent. There is also the fact that we have to compete with produce coming into the province from outside markets, particularly from our neighbours to the south. Other countries are also favoured under the export freight rate, which makes a big difference with respect to the cost of production so far as poultry, pork, beef and dairy production particularly are concerned in the province of British Columbia.
A year ago or more, I believe it was in February, the government saw fit by regulation to reduce by $5 a ton the subsidy on feed grain coming into our area, and it now becomes apparent that whereas heretofore our farmers were just able to make ends meet, they are going to have to pay an additional 7 per cent for feed, which is going to put them in a position where they just cannot carry on any longer.
In my opinion an examination of railway operation methods is desirable at this time. It is desirable because we find that the railways today are giving agreed charges to certain particular industries in order that the
Request for Election and Senate Reform railways may compete more favourably with the trucking industry and so get revenue they would otherwise lose. These agreed charges can run into the thousands, although they may not run that high at the present time, but by having more and more agreed charges it means that some other part of our economy must pay the difference between what the railways were previously getting from freight and what they are going to get in the future.
In other words, if we have a thousand agreed charges set up by the railways then products that can only be hauled by rail, such as grain or heavy steel products, must pay additional freight and thereby offset the loss under the agreed charges. During the discussion in the special committee this year of the affairs of the Canadian National Railways I remember quite well asking Donald Gordon where these agreed charges were in effect, how they became compensatory and how it was decided whether such rates applied between Hamilton and Toronto, Hamilton and Montreal, or any other two points. We always arrived at the same answer, that it was impossible to determine the exact cost from point to point. If it is impossible to determine that, how do we know that we are not losing money on agreed charges? If we are losing money on these agreed charges in order to be competitive with the trucking industry, and at the same time are taking business away from that industry, then certainly there is not sufficient derived from the grain trade at the old rate to keep up the revenue.
Therefore it becomes necessary in my opinion to examine again the problem of the railways, their handling of the business of this country and the special agreements they make with other industries in order to transport a major part of their goods and gain revenue that would otherwise go to truckers. I say that the farmer in British Columbia and in the maritimes is subsidizing the agreed charges, and we must not carry on in that fashion any longer.
It is high time we looked into this matter and stopped this indiscriminate method of just slapping on a 7 per cent or 15 per cent increase in freight rates in order to meet certain losses. It is time our railway industry woke up as to what its problem is, and it is not just the single problem of carrying freight at a nominal charge. There should be special privilege for none.
In the province of British Columbia we have other subsidiary industries that are going to be affected by the 7 per cent increase in freight rates. We have the gluten and adhesives industries. We have the edible
5352	HOUSE OF
Request for Election and Senate Reform starches, macaroni and paste foods, distillery products and other industries. With respect to the macaroni industry may I say that we had three or four factories not so many years ago that were busy all the time. Today we have but one. It is a plant which would normally keep 300 people busy. Today we find just a handful of employees working in that particular industry. The British Columbia farmers must compete with United States producers. They must compete with the foreign market completely.
We have the two freight rates. We have the domestic rate and the export rate in this country on our wheat, and this is what we find. I have a table which I took from a report given to the board of transport commissioners by the British Columbia government on February 7 of this year-it is known as Exhibit "C"-in which they take certain terminal points and discover the various costs in respect of the handling of grain. This is what we find. We find that the number of miles a car travelled to go to British Columbia was 780; the average number of tons per car was 50; and the average revenue per car was $571. These figures-the revenue figure of $571 and the mileage of 780-are important.
Transposing that, we find the following comparative rates. Exhibit "D" of that same report would indicate that on a 700 mile haul -taking other items as examples, in carload lots-aircraft parts would be carried for 700 miles for $330 as compared with $512 which might be computed on a 700-mile basis for wheat on the domestic freight rate. Ammunition pays slightly more by the carload for hauling on that same basis; it pays $660. And so we could go through this whole chart. I find, for instance, large bottles-breakable glass-being hauled over a distance of 700 miles for $369.60 while on the other hand we have $512 which must be paid for hauling wheat which is needed in order to keep our industry in operation on the west coast.
On the next page we have shown the revenue per car on coconut shells and skins, $327; ores and concentrates, $545-they too pay more-some grain products, $356; other grain, $396; hydrated lime, $320.40; old rails, $445. From studying these figures, Mr. Speaker, it becomes apparent that wheat, a commodity which is so simple to handle, is paying a rate out of all proportion as compared with that on any other product in this country for hauling to the west coast.
Exhibit "E" of this same brief deals with varying classes of freight and the distance hauled. I am just going to read one or two of these examples to illustrate the point. The chart is headed "Average revenue per car by classes compared with yield from domestic 

grain rates". First-class rate, special type, number of cars 89; revenue, $33,295; average revenue per car, $373; average haul, 731 miles. Mr. Speaker, on grain for domestic purposes, on that same basis, the revenue per car was $590. In other words we pay $217 more for the hauling of grain to be used to be fed to our stock in our poultry industry, our cattle industry and our dairying industry. Wheat pays $217 more than does the first-class freight into that particular area. The fact is that out of the ten examples we find given here, there are only two which pay more than wheat for domestic purposes.
Exhibit "G" is another of these charts which indicates a comparison of refrigerated and heated car prices as compared with domestic grain revenue. We find the cost for carrying commodities such as eggs, dressed poultry, cured meat, butter, cheese and so on. They are carried under very difficult circumstances. Yet in the case of eggs the revenue per car is $348; in the case of dressed poultry and dressed meat it is $350; cured meat, $382; butter, $320; cheese, $384; sheep, goats, cattle, hogs, $200; domestic grain, $540. In other words it costs more than twice as much to carry grain to the Pacific coast for the purpose of raising cattle and hogs than it does to send the animals themselves to the Pacific coast. That is something Mr. Speaker, that I consider is definitely wrong.
Earlier I indicated that I was opposed to the calling of an election on the premise the Leader of the Opposition indicated. While this is a particular problem that is prevalent in the province of British Columbia, and one which I am satisfied this government must examine into if they are going to keep the people of British Columbia happy and not discontented, at the same time it is not of such an extreme nature at this time, because the people in my province have not been stirred up to the degree that they feel that this government should be forced out of office after three years because they have not found a better solution to our rail problem in this country.
I would not agree that the government should permit an increase of 7 per cent in freight rates. I will not vote for such a thing. However, I am forced into the unhappy position where if I vote for the resolution I defeat my own purpose. As I said earlier, it is not in my opinion a motion of censure on the government, but is a motion of censure on democracy itself. I agree with democracy and believe in democracy; therefore as an individual I shall have to vote against the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, from listening to the young gentleman from British Columbia-and it was quite an interesting experience-I am not sure whether he realizes what he is here for. To hear him talk you would think that he was on the government benches. Judging from the remarks he has just made he does not realize that he is here for one purpose, namely as the representative of his people-a status he acquired the day after the election was over-in order to be the censor of this government and on all occasions to bring up everything necessary to throw not only this government but any government out of power after any length of time, whenever they deserve to be thrown out of power for mismanagement of the country's affairs.
He says the government are entitled, by virtue of their election, to a four-year term. Mr. Speaker, imagine a member of parliament saying that.
He was trying to be fair. You could not understand that.

If I cannot, then nobody can. I am positive you could not enlighten anybody on anything yourself. We will hear you later and let you struggle and try to demonstrate your great ability to explain anything. At the end of it nobody will know anything. Thank you.
You are welcome.

Mr. Speaker, after that rude interruption I shall proceed. I shall endeavour to teach one of that gentleman's cohorts his position in parliament. His position in the opposition is to do everything in his power to enlighten the public. If he thinks the government is wrong, whether it has been in power for a week or for four years he has the right to call for an election. He should not sit back and say they have been elected for four years, because that is not so. A government is not elected for four years or four months-
For five years.

-it is elected at the discretion of the public. The public will vote the government out if they see fit. The Leader of the Opposition has every right in the world, as has every man in this house, to call upon the Prime Minister, if he sees fit, to call an election. He may be wrong, but he has the right to say that the country has no confidence in this government and to ask the Prime Minister to adjourn the house and call an election; let the public decide. Now, the Prime Minister will decide whether or not that shall
Request for Election and Senate Reform be done, but everybody in this house has a right to voice his opinion. This closure procedure has even reached the Social Crediters. They have even closed their own mouths for a period of four years.
They were the ones who would let your member speak, when you would not; don't forget that.
I always like to let somebody speak who can speak. We have heard you speak twice during my brief-
I was just trying to help you out.
-remarks. I have been here 12 years, and I did not need your help.
It is gratis.

Everything you get for nothing is not worth a cent, so we all know what it is worth. I wish that from now on you would refrain from speaking and let the public enjoy themselves. I would think we need an opportunity to consult the people on the serious questions confronting Canada today, and for these reasons. Never in its history has Canada enjoyed the prosperity it is enjoying today.
Hear, hear.

Look who gave it to you. Look who put the oil in the Alberta sand. Look who put the iron in the rocks of Quebec. As I said before, God had nothing to do with it; they did it all.
Now, we are enjoying the greatest prosperity we have ever had. The banks in Canada have been making more money. Last year was the greatest year in their history. Industry is busy. You cannot find labour. We have a country here that deserves a population now of 16 million, and if it were not for the lack of foresight of our forefathers, my own included, this country would have had 16 million people. This country would not be looking to a foreign country to defend it. We would not be making a loan of $119 million to a foreign country to build a pipe line across Canada if our forefathers had proceeded as they should have. I am talking about my own forefathers who sat in this house and the legislatures before this.
This government has about the same kind of vision. It should have a vision for the future. It is all very well to sit back and say we are enjoying great prosperity. Is that our yardstick, that we are enjoying prosperity? The yardstick of this country, based on the natural wealth we have discovered in the last 10 years, should have no limits. Immigration has been tossed around
S354	HOUSE OF
Request for Election and Senate Reform like a wet rag by every minister this government has had since 1945. It has been the sick dog that nobody wanted; give it to the other fellow. Each one has made a greater mess of it. Here we find ourselves in a great era of prosperity saying that we must charge the man who wants to build a home in Canada more interest. We must curtail these ambitious persons. On the one hand we talk about our progress and our wealth, the position Canada holds in this world, and on the other hand we are formulating the idea of burdening the home owner. That is one reason I say the government should not be in power today, but it is not the only reason.
Then we find a man who has borrowed money from coast to coast in this country. During the period of the loan he gets a very curt letter from his bank advising him that the bank is going to raise the interest rate. In the same note they give the reason for that, practically saying that it is on orders from your government. They are not going to live up to this contract; they are going to take a half of one per cent more on the loan that they agreed upon. They are going to put another burden on his shoulders during this great period of prosperity.
We are going to stop inflation. We are going to give the stockholders of the banks of Canada additional dividends. If they do not have the dividends they are going to have permission to buy up every vacant corner in Canada and build banks on them in order to squander the earnings forced upon them by this government. That is another reason why this government should not be in power.
There is too much control in the hands of the few banks in Canada. One bank has 600 or 700 branches across Canada. They write a letter to a young man who calls himself a bank manager in an area where we might discover oil or some other commodity in a year or two, and they limit his discretion. The manager may have knowledge of the integrity of the borrower, but they impose a rule of thumb by saying to the manager, "Your limit is $1,000." If he dares exceed it he loses his job, his pension and everything else. This does not enable a man to develop his brains. This is only a suggestion, but I would suggest that all banks in Canada should be made to have a director who resides within the province, in order that the director's nose would be close to where the money is needed. These banks are controlled from Montreal or Toronto.
A gentleman may live in Saskatchewan or Alberta because he believes that is the best place in which to live. He may go to IMr. Ferguson.]

the bank manager to borrow money but the bank manager will say, "No matter how much I feel you are worth, no matter how much I know from general observation that you will succeed, I can only lend you $500. I must send a letter down to head office to get you $625." It is a time for expansion in our great country. It is time a great country like Canada broke those shackles and went on with the prosperity that God gave us. Do not do like our forefathers did. There were many things we adopted from the old country that were great anchors and formed great foundations, and we should still remember them and use them for all they are worth, but we should develop some new ideas. This is a new country so far as development is concerned.
We should have an official in charge of immigration who is scheming and planning and successfully bringing immigrants of all classes and creeds into this country. We are short of labour in Canada today. We are lacking good competition owing to the shortage of labour. This country has been built largely on immigrants, the type who work. Surely when we are at the height of our prosperity that is not the time to tell the world we do not want them. We have missed the boat-
That is why you just got back.

-on first class, selected people who have wanted to come here in the past 10 years. What is happening today? The people we wanted, the people we needed, are not permitted to leave their own countries because those countries are so busy. The present government had not faith enough to see or believe that this country would need manpower. Now we are curtailing construction. The brains that should be used in progress are now being used to curtail construction. Today the Minister of Finance spoke about 2J per cent interest rates in New York and 3 per cent rates in Minnesota. What has Minnesota to do with the Dominion of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Because of the federal reserve bank. That is what I was talking about.

Let me say this to the Minister of Finance. The banks of Canada will not take and pay interest on millions of European dollars that want to come out here for investment purposes. That is the situation. I would ask the Minister of Finance whether he can tell this house right now if any foreign bank or citizen wishes to deposit with or lend to any Canadian bank the sum of $2 million, will they pay 1J per cent on that money? Can the minister answer that question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will not answer it now.

I know they will not, and I believe the minister knows they will not, but he is not quite sure and therefore he is quite right not to answer. I know they will not take a deposit of $1 million from a foreigner and pay him 1-J per cent interest. We are short of capital and foreigners want to invest in this country, but the banks will not pay interest on the money. The Bank of Canada should take that money and lend it to further justifiable projects.
That is the reason I call this government a gumbo government. May I say to those who do not know what it means that in the western provinces there is a soil that when you get into it you get mired and you cannot go anywhere. Progress stops. This government reminds me of a democrat and a pair of horses on the prairie out in the gumbo. They cannot get out and they cannot go any farther. They are gumboed by prosperity. Their great effort is to get out of the prosperity by increasing the interest rates, by decreasing the loans and by working in with the United States and charging a rate of interest equal to that charged in Montana. Montana is not Canada. Montana is not enjoying the prosperity of Canada. Montana has not the riches Canada has. There is no resemblance in the two pictures.
We are a nation on our own, and it is time we took the bit in our teeth and went forward. I am a Canadian who loves this country; I am a Canadian who wants my people to go forward. Whenever I hear of a discovery of natural resources I say, "This is my Canada". When I see shackles put on people in any way, shape or form, and on young people who are the future leaders in this country, I say this government has been in office long enough and I shall do everything within my power to see that it goes out as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, in supporting the motion of the Leader of the Opposition that this government has lost the confidence of the people of Canada, I intend to show that this is particularly true in the maritime provinces. The New Brunswick election of June 18 has come and gone, and a great many things will be read into the sweeping Conservative victory of that day. I suppose some will say it was the personality of the premier and the other candidates. Others may say it was organization.
No; it was Tom Bell.

The hon. member for Charlotte has certainly an awful lot of nerve to make 67509-339
Request for Election and Senate Reform any reference at all to the New Brunswick election after what he said.
Mr. Speaker, I must rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member for Charlotte said not a word.
Don't blow your top. I did not say a word.

All I can say to the Minister of Public Works is that he may get his own due in Nova Scotia some time this year or next spring. I do apologize to the hon. member for Charlotte, because I know he would be much wiser than to say anything.
On a question of privilege; it is not that I would be much wiser not to say anything. The fact is, I did not say anything. I shall have something to say later.

Will you call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

I should just like to clarify the record in this respect.
Mr. Speaker, before supper I did not do very well-
Hear, hear.

-in my reference to an interruption. I confused the Lunenburg twang of the Minister of Public Works and the American-influenced drawl of the hon. member for Charlotte with a well-known interrupter from the western provinces, and I wish to apologize for referring to them in that regard.
As I was saying, however, the New Brunswick election was perhaps not a great surprise but it did show the feeling we have in New Brunswick toward the interest of the present federal government. No individual, with the possible exception of the premier, had a great bearing or influence on the results, and I think there was a noticeable trend as the election approached toward the attention or lack of attention we get in New Brunswick and the maritimes generally from the federal government.
If an election were called, Mr. Speaker, as is suggested by the Leader of the Opposition in his motion, I say that New Brunswick, and I think the other maritime provinces, would vote against this government and its so-called policies. It is not so much the discrimination and the lack of attention, perhaps, as the runaround we get with our proposals. Then afterwards comes the old salt in our wounds treatment, and it is rubbed into us as we go along trying to catch the elusive bait. It is somewhat like losing a deposit at election time when you know you did not have a chance anyway.
There is some history to this and I could go back over quite a few years, but the point I have in mind is illustrated very nicely by a statement made by the Prime Minister recently to the labour convention at Toronto. I was at this convention sitting there listening to his remarks on labour, and all of a sudden out of the blue came a reference by the Prime Minister to the maritime economic situation. I do not have the exact report, but the press quotes the Prime Minister as using these words:
.	.	. economic redevelopment of the Atlantic
provinces deserves consideration.


That was the first reference; later on the Prime Minister said:
. . . special measures should perhaps be taken to improve the economy of the Atlantic provinces. This merits and is receiving attention from many of us. However, the initiative and the ideas, the energies and the determination to accomplish this redevelopment cannot originate in other parts of Canada; they must come from the Atlantic area.
The first part, where the Prime Minister recognizes the fact that we do need consideration in our economic development, is appreciated. We marvel at the innocent candor of it; we marvel at the fact that the Prime Minister is so late in recognizing this need; we wonder where his advice has been. We appreciate that these are the words of the Prime Minister, and the intention must be taken for granted. The respect the Prime Minister held at that time was possibly a little different from what it is now, but I have no quarrel with the thought behind those words.
The second part of the statement does give me some difficulty. First of all there is the fact that the Prime Minister suggests that we do not have and have not shown the initiative and energy in the past; that is confusing to me, and I could not let that part of his statement go unchallenged. There is also the fact that all the initiative must come from the maritimes rather than Ottawa itself showing some interest; that is another part of his statement the tone and inference of which I do not like. There is the further implication in his words that we must again come to Ottawa, when we decide what we have in mind, with our hat in hand. I do not like that principle, Mr. Speaker.
When the proposal was made and when we heard about it in the maritimes, there was generally a good response to it and it was a non-political response; I want that on the record. The premiers of all the provinces have shown a willingness to get together to see what can be done. They take this as a good omen for the future. The various boards of trade, the maritime transportation commission and A.P.E.C., the new Atlantic provinces economic council, have all increased their own interest as well. Even the few Liberals who are left in the opposition in New Brunswick have shown an interest in this and have gone on record as supporting it. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, I cannot let the latter part of the Prime Minister's words go unchallenged when he suggests that energies and initiative have been lacking in the past, and that we must come again with our hat in hand to Ottawa.
I ask the house tonight, Mr. Speaker, has the Prime Minister not heard of our efforts in the past with respect to various phases of

federal aid? Has the Prime Minister not heard of Passamaquoddy, that project between New Brunswick and the United States that harnesses the tides which would give us power, the dream of the fabulous Dexter Cooper of the 1920's? The United States government have not followed along as well as they should, but they are moving on it. Canada now is forced to take part at least in investigations of that project.
Has the Prime Minister not heard of the Chignecto canal project, that shortcut between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick that would mean so much to coastwise trade, that project that has been talked about since the late nineteenth century?
Has the Prime Minister not heard of our efforts to obtain atomic power plants in the maritimes? Nova Scotia, hard up as it is for power, approached the federal government very early in the proceedings with a request that it be given first consideration for an atomic plant there. New Brunswick is on the list, too, but what happened? It went to Ontario again. We are still on the list.
How about the dominion-provincial conference? Does the Prime Minister not remember the proposals we made there? Nova Scotia and New Brunswick again were in substantial agreement on the fiscal need factor. They asked only that the income of the maritimes be brought up to 85 per cent of the national average. Surely that is not too much to ask. That was another proposal about which it would appear the Prime Minister did not hear.
How about the coal industry and the efforts that have been made by Nova Scotia to obtain some help there? How about the request that we have made so many times for protection, for the protected industries to use Canadian ports instead of New York and other United States ports? How about the request we made for consideration for defence industry? Has the Prime Minister not heard of those proposals? Does he suggest, in his words to the labour convention at Toronto, that we did not make efforts during the war and afterward to obtain some defence industry?
Then, of course, there are the various appeals that have been made by the members from the maritimes over the years. I think those words are almost an insult to the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), 21 years here, speaking time and time again of the various needs. Yet it would appear that the Prime Minister had never heard of any of them, when he said at the Toronto convention that the initiative and energy must come from ourselves.
25, 1956	5357
Request for Election and Senate Reform
Then, of course, there is the final red herring and the final smokescreen with regard to the request of the New Brunswick government to obtain much-needed financial assistance for its power development. I refer specifically to the Beechwood project. I am going to take a minute to dwell on this, to show the way this government has confused and misled everybody with respect to this. We came up here in 1952 or thereabouts with this Beechwood proposal. True, we may not have been definite at that time. It was impossible to be definite about some of the various financial requirements that we might have, but it was an unpartisan approach. We gave credit to the old Liberal government in the province, which made some of the initial investigation.
We came here, we thought we saw the right people and we did the best we could. The thing has gone on and on. It reminds me of a fisherman who has a baited hook. Just as we get up to it, it is pulled a little further away and we lose sight of it. Then of course, the bait has been changed on the hook, and there have been different fishermen. I come to three statements that I think are pertinent and show the confusion that exists. They show the way the maritimes are misled and mixed up in these matters. We came up here with this Beechwood project, a project that is similar to the seaway and the pipe line. We have been all through that. This is the treatment we got. There were no efforts made in the house by the responsible ministers from New Brunswick or from the other parts of the maritimes on the treasury benches. The first we heard about it was in a radio broadcast made some two years ago by the Minister of Labour, and this is what he said about our request.
Labour Minister Gregg told New Brunswick by radio Sunday the federal government can't help the province finance the Beechwood hydroelectric project on the St. John river.
He said in his report from Parliament Hill that since confederation such matters have been reserved to the provinces.
There is the first reference. The Minister of Labour, our representative from New Brunswick in the federal cabinet, fell back on constitutional grounds.
The next reference that is important came on January 26 this year, when the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), asked a question of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage). I shall not go into the question, but it dealt with the possibility of obtaining co-operation, and particularly financial co-operation, in the development of the Saint John river. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National
5358	HOUSE OF
Request for Election and Senate Reform Resources at that time fell back on the fact that we had not made a substantial request. I have the latest request here, and it certainly seems definite to me. That was another red herring and another act of confusion.
The final outrage in the whole treatment by the cabinet of this serious request of ours, which meant so much for our future, was given by the Prime Minister on May 8 in answer to a question by the hon. member for Royal. The Prime Minister at that time- I do not know whether it was through ignorance or in a deliberate attempt to confuse the issue again-referred to the fact that a loan had been undertaken. There has not been any loan undertaken by anybody, as far as I can find out, in connection with Beechwood. Then the discussion went on with respect to the loan for the Beechwood project. The Beechwood project has not been financed; the provincial government have gone ahead with it but they are meeting the cost from year to year out of their ordinary capital commitments.
I say that because I think it shows the confusion this government has always attempted to convey in connection with any legitimate requests of the maritime provinces. I mention this seriously because I feel that it is the reason there is such growing unrest in the maritimes against the policies of this government.
All the time the ministers were making these statements, the deputy minister of finance, in open letters to the government, was suggesting that it was economically feasible that Beechwood be proceeded with. Then the other part of the government which deals with such matters, the joint commission headed by General McNaughton, had this to say. In the committee on external affairs last year General McNaughton said that, as an individual, he saw no reason why Ottawa should not help New Brunswick in obtaining power. He said:
After all. what have we got confederation for?
These are the reasons why, if an election were held tomorrow, the people of New Brunswick would show their indignation. Then I have another quotation from General McNaughton yesterday:
The rapid construction of Beechwood following the recommendation of the international joint commission was a courageous act.
He gives us credit. A servant of the crown gives us credit for going ahead and attempting this development on our own. I suggest that this new statement the Prime Minister has made is another smokescreen and another red herring. We are taking advantage of it because we do not want to be accused of missing anything. I hope there is sincerity


and good intention behind it, but I say to all the members in attendance this evening that if this house were dissolved tomorrow and an election held, the province of New Brunswick would vote 100 per cent against this government and the lack of attention they have given to our proposals. I would be willing to wager that the other maritime provinces would vote substantially the same way.
Put up your money.

What is the reason behind this, Mr. Speaker? There is only one reason. The government has failed to recognize that Canada's resources should be developed by Canadians in every part of Canada. That is the crux of the whole complaint. There is a serious undertone in the air in the maritimes today. It is the reason Premier Hugh John Flemming was returned in the New Brunswick provincial election last week. He recognizes the principle that this government does not appreciate for one minute. That principle concerns the development of the resources of our province. The federal government does not appreciate that it should assist in such development in every part of this country.
The principle was established when we assisted jointly with the trans-Canada pipe line. It was also enunciated in the same degree when we went along with federal assistance to the St. Lawrence seaway. We have come forward now with our request, and it bears repeating and repeating because some people here cannot seem to understand what we want and they seem to throw up roadblocks and smokescreens. We want the same consideration in our part of the country that these other sections of the country are now receiving. I say that has not been given to us.
I go along with the motion of the Leader of the Opposition that the house should be dissolved so the people can voice their indignation against such sectional, discriminatory policies. This is the same old Liberalism to me. I do not care if it is Liberalism in New Brunswick or Liberalism across Canada. It is that Liberalism that thrives on sectionalism, on playing one part of the country against the other. We saw it in the election in New Brunswick. They pitted Saint John against Fredericton, one end of the country against the other, and when they attempt to do it in Canada by assisting in developing one part and not developing others it has the same old smell to me.
Finally, I say the government are on the wrong track. They refuse to recognize that this is a great country. We have a great future, and we have to go along with it. If

the maritimes only want 85 per cent of the national average income I say they should get it, and we are going to voice our opinions this fall if this motion does not go through.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I feel I must say a few words. The Leader of the Opposition made a speech this afternoon, part of which I listened to and the other part of which I have read. He spoke about Senate reform. He spoke about proceedings in the Senate and proceedings in this house, and concluded with a motion which reads as follows:
In the opinion of this house the Prime Minister should give immediate consideration to the advisability of bringing about the dissolution of this parliament and the calling of a general election as soon as possible.
I have listened reverently to the speech just made by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. He spoke of several projects which are of great interest to his native province and to the maritime provinces generally. I did not hear him say anything about the main subject which led to the motion that was moved as a grievance. I heard him refer to the Beechwood project, which I think was one of the hydroelectric projects included in a grievance motion earlier this session together with other similar projects, and therefore a matter which had already been discussed. But 1 will grant him this, that there might have been some new facts come to light since and therefore it might have been worth while airing them. But I am in the same position as I was in 1955. I see that citation 467 says:
Whenever an order of the day has been read for the house to resolve itself into the committee of supply or the committee of ways and means, the motion "That the Speaker do now leave the chair" must be proposed, except on Thursday and Friday as provided by standing order 28.
That part has been changed by a new standing order. Anyway, I continue:
When such motion is proposed, it shall be permissible to discuss any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament or to ask for the redress of any grievance, and it is not necessary to move an amendment for that purpose; provided that the discussion and the amendment, if one is moved, shall not relate to any decision of the house during the current session, nor to any item of the estimates, nor to any resolution to be proposed to the committee of ways and means, nor to any matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper.
Then citation 468 reads:
It sometimes happens, on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for committee of supply, that members air grievances without moving amendments. A member may speak on railway rates, another on naturalization, and so on. Five or six different matters may then be brought to the government's attention. But no member is allowed to speak more than once on the motion. He cannot discuss all the matters which may then come up, and when he has spoken on one of them
25, 1956	5359
Request for Election and Senate Reform he has exhausted his right to speak to the motion before the house, namely, "That the Speaker do now leave the chair".
It appears to me that if we are to follow the subjects that have been introduced so far during the debate, which is supposed to be one on a specific grievance, we can speak about Senate reform, we can speak about proceedings in this house and the proceedings in the Senate on the pipe-line bill, we can speak on all the projects which are of interest to the maritime provinces, as outlined by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, and there may have been other hon. members who have spoken and discussed other matters but whom I did not have the chance to listen to because I was absent from the chair from 3.30 until six o'clock.
Hon. members will remember that in 1955 the hon. member for Prince Albert made a speech on wheat and concluded with a motion having to do with the South Saskatchewan river dam. Members were puzzled. They did not know what they were going to speak about, whether they could speak on the South Saskatchewan river dam or on wheat or on both subjects at the same time. An arrangement was reached at that time whereby we would deal with the river dam project and later with wheat. That discussion of order, as it took place, appears at pages 3790 and 3791 of Hansard of May 16, 1955.
I expressed the view at that time that we should not get into another budget debate. I realize that this is the fifth supply motion and that there is just one left. Supply motions are opposition motions; they are want of confidence motions. There is no doubt in my mind that this amendment, as it is brought forward at the moment and as it is being interpreted by those who have taken part in the debate, does take in too much territory. In other words, during the rest of today and tomorrow we can have on this motion a miniature budget debate, and all this for the purpose of calling an election.
There is another point I want to warn the house against, and it is the terms of the motion itself. Should this motion carry the house would resolve that in the opinion of this house the Prime Minister should give immediate consideration to the advisability of bringing about the dissolution of this parliament and the calling of a general election as soon as possible. I do not make this a major point, but I submit it to hon. members.
There are certain prerogatives attached to the office of the Prime Minister, and one of those is to advise that parliament be dissolved and a general election be called. According to the citations I have just read, is this matter, that is the exercise of the
5360	HOUSE OF
Request for Election and Senate Reform prerogative of the Prime Minister, one which comes within the jurisdiction of the house or is it one which comes within the category of affairs within the administration of the government?
I have made these observations not for the purpose of ruling the amendment out of order and not for the purpose of curtailing the discussion, but merely to warn that in the future if a similar motion were to be made under similar circumstances, with a speech of a certain type leading to the motion and other members speaking on many other subject matters; if it should come up again I may be in a position to deal with it. I hope that in the meantime I shall have had a chance to study the situation as it is presented and perhaps make a ruling.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the last
speaker was addressing the house I was of course reminded of the fact that both he and I are interested in certain parts of the country where there have been elections recently.
Not with the same result.
While he had the privilege of assisting a government back into office, I had the opportunity to try to put one out, but was not successful.
That is putting it mildly.

I took a considerable part in that campaign and was pleased to find, when I got back, that one of the important duties I performed while there brought forth quite an editorial in the local Conservative paper. I may say to begin with that the editor of the local paper is a personal friend of mine, in spite of the fact that we do not belong to the same political party.
He took the trouble to point out that I had been putting up bills. After all, putting up bills is an important part of a campaign, as a rule; and I must admit that I spent part of my time in putting up bills. But I had another matter in mind rather than just the matter of putting up bills. In the days when I came into politics first we had only two parties in Canada. When we put up bills our opposition left them up and when our opposition put up bills, we left them up. But in recent years we have had the experience that when we put up bills, they seemed to disappear; and I had the idea that maybe somebody took them down. Hence when I was out there in the campaign this time I took some equipment along with me


and I put up a few bills myself. Then I drove around again the day after the election and I found that they were still all up.
I do not know whether or not it was some C.C.F. friend who reported back to Ottawa that I was out putting up bills and who might have been following me around, but I simply want to say that I am in doubt now as to whether the wind took the bills down in the past or whether somebody pulled them down. Those I put up-and I put them up in the proper way-stayed up. In that particular part of the country no C.C.F.'er was elected, so the bills might have had some effect.
The resolution before the house at the present time suggests that this government should go to the country. The motion of the Leader of the Opposition was as follows:
I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Diefenbaker: "That all the words after 'That' to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
in the opinion of this house the Prime Minister should give immediate consideration to the advisability of bringing about the dissolution of this parliament and the calling of a general election as soon as possible."
Your last remarks, Mr. Speaker, remind me of the fact that our system of government sets up a method under which elections must be called. The fact is that the only one who can form a government is an individual in the house who can command a majority of the membership of the house. It does not make any difference whether they are elected as Conservatives, C.C.F.'ers, Social Crediters, Liberals or what. If there is any individual in the house who can command a majority he is entitled to form a government, and he does so.
At the present time an appeal is made- and one was made the other day-to the Prime Minister to call an election. Surely there is not anyone in this house who contends that there is any other person in the house who can command a majority except the Prime Minister.
Go to the people and find out.

Judging by what has happened in the past I think he would have good reason for believing that there is not much likelihood of an election bringing about any different result, namely that after the election the present Prime Minister would be the only one who could form a government.
Wishful thinking.

Hence nothing much is going to be gained by yielding to the suggestion that we have an election.

The motion is based upon some remarks which were made by the Leader of the Opposition. He referred to a debate which had taken place in this house, but I think he lived within the rules in not quoting the debate and not trying to say what had been said during the debate. Probably that was just as well from his point of view, because in the period that I was here while that discussion was taking place I do not remember that anyone on the other side of the house said much about the pipe-line bill.
Oh, oh.

Some of my hon. friends are beginning to look up their notes. If they said anything about the pipe-line bill, it was only for the purpose of hanging on it a point of order or something else in order to get a vote.
Nonsense.

That is one reason that is referred to as giving background for the calling of an election. The other is the possibility that something might have happened over in the Senate that gives some reason for discussion.
Something will happen over there.
Let us see just what happened.
Nothing has happened there in years.

Here is one thing that happened in the Senate:
If the house is not agreeable to third reading now, I suggest that we meet tomorrow morning at eleven o'clock. I do not want the charge to be laid against this house that the bill was forced through in one day. That just is not done.
Those are the words of the leader of the opposition in the Senate.
They forced it through in two days.

Then he went on to say this:
With the consent of the house may I say a word before we adjourn? I wish to thank the leader of the government for the splendid way in which he has conducted this committee of the whole. It has been a very great pleasure to all of us.
Apparently the leader of the opposition in the Senate does not agree with the Leader of the Opposition in this house. He maintains that the discussions were what was expected in the Senate, and he thanks the leader of the government in the Senate for having so conducted those discussions. I venture to say that the leader of the opposition in the
Request for Election and Senate Reform other place is not so much concerned about an election as is the Leader of the Opposition in this house.
This afternoon we listened to an outline of the democratic system as we enjoy it in this country, and the opinion was expressed by the Leader of the Opposition and by some others who have spoken that the conduct of the house during a certain period was not such as to inspire confidence in our system in the minds of people in Canada or outside of Canada.
In making these statements the Leader of the Opposition referred continuously to the subservient members of that part of the parliament of Canada, subservient to the members of this house, subservient to the members of the government. I submit, Mr. Speaker, if there is any term that should not be applied to the members of the Senate, it would be that term. I am inclined to think that during most of the discussion on the point, what we have considered to be the rule laid down with regard to mention of what goes on in the other place, although it is not a hard and fast rule, has been lived up to by members in this house and members in other houses where you have a secondary chamber. They do not make references to individuals or to the house as a whole such as were made here this afternoon. I wish to take some objection to those remarks having been made.
Our democratic system, as everyone in this house knows, is based upon the experiences they have had in the centre of the empire, in Britain. Those experiences run over a long term of years. The statement is made that our system of government is built up from precedent to precedent, and that is true. Practically everything which takes place in this house or in the parliament of the United Kingdom has also taken place at some previous time, and whatever is proper to do now has been established as a precedent. We go on doing things in accordance with those precedents.
So we have here the Commons and the Senate, and in the Commons we introduce legislation. Sometimes we introduce it in the Senate, but in this particular case it was introduced in this house. During the discussion members have been raising some objection to the fact that in the debate on the pipe-line bill the opposition took one point of view and the government party took another. This is the common thing in a house constituted as this is. On this occasion, of course, two of the opposition parties opposed the action taken by the government and one party agreed. The Prime Minister, therefore, in this particular action had more
5362	HOUSE OF
Request for Election and Senate Reform support than he has on ordinary questions that come before this house. On other occasions he has only had the support of the members of the Liberal party. He can only rest assured that he is going to have that support in the future.
Before the hon. member for New Westminster spoke on behalf of the Social Credit group just before dinner with regard to the matter there were very few, if any, on this side of the house who knew just how the Social Credit group might vote on this particular question. In other words, while they have supported this side of the house on the bill itself there was no particular reason why, on a motion of want of confidence in the government, they should be bound to support the government now. But at least one member of that party has indicated here that he intends to do so. He is not going to support the motion that this parliament be brought to a close and an election held. I presume there will be others who will do the same. I repeat, therefore, there is no indication in this house that the Prime Minister cannot control a majority of the house in connection with this or any of the other questions that may come before the house in the immediate future.
The opposition has stated time after time in this debate that the rules are made to protect the opposition. Well, that may be correct; and I will agree that they need some protection, Mr. Speaker. The rules may be made to protect the opposition. I think, as a matter of fact, they are made to protect all the members of the house.
They are broken to protect the government.

It would require a very peculiar kind of rule to protect the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis). He just rushes in where angels fear to tread. Nevertheless he has a right to do whatever he feels like doing in the house, I suppose, as long as he stays within the rules. The rules of this house are simply based upon common sense. One does not need to study the rule book too much to know whether he is in order or out of order.
There are one or two members on this side of the house who may take offence at what I am going to say. I have sometimes thought if Cecil Rhodes had his life to live over again he would not send Rhodes scholars over to Oxford. One of the reasons I have come to that conclusion is that in watching the actions of certain members of this house I have noticed that the more time they have spent in a university the more difficulty we have in understanding just why they do certain things. As a matter of fact the only


fellow who has done this, and whom I can really understand, is my friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). He was in college when I started, and he was still there when I came out.
Oh, oh.

However, that was not because he was not passing his examinations but because he went through an arts course and then went through a course in theology. He was there just twice as long as I was because he went through that particular course.
I see my friend on the other side of the house who has done a similar thing, and I see another gentleman sitting across the aisle from him who was a Rhodes scholar. I am reminded that both of them spent most of the early part of their lives studying the rules in mock parliaments in a university somewhere, and they have been applying that idea to the running of this house during this session. You know, when we used to have mock parliaments in university-it does not make any difference where it was-our chief objective was to learn the rules. There was not anything else we could do anyway. We could not pass any laws that had any effect upon anybody, so we made a study of the rules by moving this and moving that, moving points of order and keeping everybody het up over something.

You had
closure, then, I suppose.

We had a demonstration of that in this house during this session. It was nothing more than that. I must say that I did not stay for all of it, but I did stay for half of it. During the time I was here I did make a speech on the bill, and I am sure none of my friends opposite read it because they were not interested in the bill at all. They were only interested in these points of order that they could bring up in order to take up all the time.
Someone says that public opinion was such and such as a result of this. Well, not being here but being out in the country I had a better opportunity of learning what public opinion was on the question. I had occasion to talk to people from time to time and learn what they were really thinking. You know, when I did discuss these matters with people from time to time I found they did not hold the same opinion as the hon. member who just sat down thinks they hold. I must say that out in the country where I was they did not vote for the government party either.
I do believe, though, there is a considerable number of people in Canada who believe that

the old tradition, which is historical in this country, still lives. This old historical tradition is that it is easier for a provincial government to get elected when the federal government is on the other side of the fence. I think that is true, and has been true over the years. Probably our friends who are suggesting that because certain things happened over the country in connection with these provincial elections, that indicates some reason why the situation which exists is still going to exist when we have another federal election.
I am quite sure that is not the case. My hon. friends would be well advised not to build up their hopes too much, because an election will roll around soon enough. I am quite sure it will come a few months earlier than they expect it, and a few months earlier than is good for them when it does come.
We have had these men asking the government to resign, and my friends keep shouting "closure". What is the situation with regard to rules? There was a considerable time in different parts of the world when they copied the British form of government, whether it was within the commonwealth or outside of it, and tried to carry on in the same manner as they did in Britain. In all these countries they had rules, and those rules were made, as has been said, to protect the interests of the opposition. But in all those countries they eventually found that the tendency to take advantage of situations which might develop is not confined to government parties. It can be just as prevalent among opposition parties, and so other rules had to be added.
When people on the other side of the house talk about the rules having been used for certain purposes, they lose sight of the fact that such procedure as that was followed by practically every country where there is a democratic government. Some procedure of closure on debate is in force in most of the legislative bodies of the world, notably in Great Britain, Italy, France, Germany, The Netherlands, Portugal, Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Spain, Switzerland and in the United States House of Representatives.
Now, this is a pretty complete list of the nations that have democratic governments and all of them have found it necessary to have a closure rule. Why have they found it necessary to have a closure rule?
