I should like to see their faces when they meet him out in the country in the next election campaign. They will be the most downcast individuals who will be met from one end of this country to the other. Just as in the past, they will find that the people of Canada have the same confidence in him now as they had on the two previous occasions-
We shall see.

-on one of which they gave him the greatest majority any party ever had in this house up to that time, and on the next occasion they increased it. I think they will increase it again whenever they get an opportunity to do so.

As to development in this country, may I say this. Not only every person in this country but every person of any importance in the United States, in Britain and in the countries over the world knows that there is no comparison between the development that has taken place in this country during the last 10 years and that in any other 10 years in its history. During the past 10 years this country has grown into a nation recognized by all the countries in the world as one of the outstanding nations. We shall carry that reputation down to the next election, at which time I am sure we shall carry ourselves through at the polls and leave a few of our friends sitting on the other side of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention and great interest to the diffuse and rambling speech made by the Minister of Agriculture, who I understand is tonight Acting Prime Minister, and which dealt so fully with bill posting, parliamentary procedure, Saskatchewan politics and the pugilistic ability of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). I am not going to be like the minister and break the rules. I am, as usual, going to keep to the rules and apply my remarks to the amendment that is now under discussion.
I rise this evening particularly to bring to the attention of the house the neglect of this government in one respect of about 5,000 of my constituents. I have done it a number of times throughout the years, but I do so tonight again because I think this is an opportunity to focus attention on this injustice that about 5,000 of my constituents have suffered for some 30 years. Satisfactory radio reception has been available to the majority of Canadians for about 30 years; but, as I said before, I have about 5,000 constituents who are unable to hear Canadian radio during the greater portion of the 24 hours.
They are lucky.

I say that is unjust. We can spend millions of dollars on television and on the improvement of television. That is something I do not regret, though on two or three evenings when I looked at a program .-I forget the name of it just now-on which they produce some rather queer plays from Toronto I thought that if they would spend the money it cost to produce one of these plays in assisting my constituents to enjoy radio, it would be to the better advantage of this country.
These people, Mr. Speaker, have a real grievance, and this is a time for bringing grievances to the attention of the house. That is why I raise it again. I have raised it year after year without results. The area affected
Request for Election and Senate Reform -and I know there are other areas; there are,
I think, about eight or ten other areas in Canada-that suffers in a similar way, and of which I am speaking, is the greater part of the Arrow lakes area, the north Kootenay area and the Slocan lake area. While other Canadians have been enjoying Canadian radio, these people for 30 years have been unable to enjoy radio the greater part of the time.
I know that in order to overcome that situation low-power relay stations have been erected at Castlegar and Kaslo. That move has been much appreciated by the people who are affected. But this area of which I am speaking is still as it was 30 years ago, and that is why I raise the question this evening.
When I went into this question some half dozen years ago I said, "Is the situation caused by unusual radio interference?" I took it up with the then minister of transport, Mr. Chevrier, who very kindly agreed that he would have a thorough investigation made of the whole area by the officials of his department, and he did so. After that investigation was completed I received this letter, which indicated that the major trouble was not radio interference, although there is considerable of that. I read from the letter dated May 30, 1952:
The provision of reliable radio reception throughout British Columbia is a very difficult problem. The mountainous terrain, which absorbs the daytime radio waves travelling along the ground, prevents reliable daytime reception in such areas. As a result radio signals are not strong enough to be clearly heard above the normal, irreducible background of radio noise from electrical sources and atmospherics. At night distant radio signals which travel far above the earth and are reflected back to earth by the ionisphere, cause interference to local stations occupying the same channels. There are in the neighbourhood of 3,000 broadcast stations on the North American continent, operating on only 107 channels. Thus there is considerable interference between stations transmitting on the same channel where the desired signal is weak.
For instance Nakusp is not within the primary service area of any Canadian station. Nighttime secondary service may sometimes be had from Trail, Kelowna or Penticton, with occasional reception from CBE Vancouver or CBX Lacombe, but signal strengths are found to be very low.
It is therefore apparent that the poor radio reception in Kootenay West is due to inadequate signal strength, and is not generally caused by excessive interference from electrical sources. In many areas which suffer in this manner, the C.B.C. has installed "booster" stations which are located at repeater points on the wire networks and which afford broadcast service to local communities where they are situated.
So we cleared that up, Mr. Speaker. I can speak from personal experience on this matter, because I live miles away from anyone else. There is no road access to my home, and my nearest neighbour on one side is seven miles

Request for Election and Senate Reform away and 12 miles on the other. We therefore depend on the radio. One evening my daughters were trying to tune in some station and a United States station came in. They said, "Well, Daddy, we have got Charlie McCarthy." I said, "It cannot be Charlie McCarthy because he comes on Sunday evenings." They were insistent upon that, so we listened to that program for about 10 minutes. Then when it came to a conclusion we heard the announcer say, "You have been listening to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) broadcast from Lethbridge." I mention that to indicate the difficulty in radio reception in our area.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this matter is of such consequence that it has been studied by all types of organizations in the area; the chambers of commerce, the boards of trade of southwestern British Columbia. They have taken up the matter and have asked the federal government to have a survey made of our district. This was last year. It has been discussed at many of their meetings. The local chambers of commerce in Kootenay West that are affected, boards of trade, farmers' institutes and women's institutes have had meetings and passed resolutions, but so far without effect. Then the local people have had petitions signed which I have sent to the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Hundreds of people have written letters concerning these circumstances. In addition to that, those who operate air services in the area have written pointing out that they are unable to receive weather bulletins and on that account their flying is made much more difficult.
Now, in order to indicate the situation-and I bring it up because this is an unfair situation to these people-I am going to quote from one resolution that I received recently, which was sent to the chairman of the broadcasting corporation. This was a resolution passed unanimously by the Nakusp chamber of commerce. I might say here that is one of the beauty spots on the Arrow lakes, a very active, progressive and growing community. The resolution reads:
Whereas the geographical location of Nakusp and its surrounding area is such that it is impossible to get satisfactory radio reception; and Whereas it does not appear possible to build Canadian stations of sufficient power to overcome those American stations in California and Seattle which are of the same wave length; and,
Whereas the Canadian government is spending millions of dollars each year to provide television to people who have excellent radio reception; and,
Whereas it is not possible to consistently receive Canadian news, Canadian civil defence instructions or warnings, Canadian political broadcasts or any Canadian cultural programs; and,
Whereas as Canadians we feel that we have the right to know what is happening in Canada; and,

Whereas the farmers of this district need the Canadian weather forecast if they are to properly take care of their crops; and,
Whereas the farmers of this district need the Canadian market news; and.
Whereas other areas and communities of less population are at the present time satisfactorily serviced by C.B.C. booster stations:
Therefore be it resolved that this chamber of commerce recommend to the board of governors of the C.B.C. the installation of a booster station at Nakusp to serve the needs of the people in this area.
I just read that resolution to indicate they are concerned about this matter. It would not take more than three booster stations, one at Nakusp, one at Rosebery, and one at Balfour. To these repeated representations from organizations, petitions and letters, Mr. Dunton has replied in each case, and I am going to read his latest reply in this connection. He says in part:
As we have explained before the difficulty about filling in some of the gaps in our coverage is that of finance. As matters stand now the outlook is that we shall be short of funds even to carry on existing services and it will be a question not of expanding but of reducing. It is possible, however, that some adjustment will be made in the methods of financing the sound broadcasting system, and with that in mind the corporation is going ahead with further study of coverage needs, and the costs involved, including southeastern British Columbia.
So we are told it is a matter of financing. I understand that nothing will be done to remedy this situation until a report is received from the royal commission on broadcasting. Well, it is unfair to ask these people to wait that long.
Then quite recently the present Minister of Transport had a survey made of the area to see if there was a great deal of interference that could be overcome by various measures. They come to the same conclusion, I think. There were three officials from the Department of Transport who made the survey in the area, and this is what they say according to a letter received from the deputy minister of transport, Mr. Brassard, dated May 9, 1956.
The report indicates that the main reason for the complaints is not that the interference level is high, but rather that the strength of the broadcast signals received is extremely low throughout the Nakusp area due to the terrain.
That applies to the whole area.
In the circumstances, it is not always possible to suppress interference to the point where satisfactory reception is attained, however, our staff will take all reasonable measures to eliminate preventible sources.
We appreciate what is being done in that respect. They did discover some sources of interference.
We are given to understand that the Nakusp board of trade had previously approached the C.B.C. for the installation of a low-powered

broadcast relay station in Nakusp, but that the request was turned down because program carrying lines were not available. It is reported that such lines are now available and that the board is making a new application.
I read that to indicate it is still not a question of interference but the low strength of the signals. We have Canadian Pacific lines going in which were not available some three or four years ago. The poles were old and the lines almost obsolete. Since that time there have been some severe storms and the Canadian Pacific has taken advantage of the situation to rebuild the line, so they are now in a position to give a wire service between Nelson and Rosebery and Nelson and Nakusp. There is also at the present time a B.C. telephone line between Nelson and Kaslo, and we would only have to take a feeder line off to serve Balfour, Procter, Crawford Bay and the Kootenay lake area.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this does not seem a serious matter to people who enjoy good radio reception. In my opinion it does seem unfair that those people who are producing such a great amount of wealth should be denied the opportunity to listen to Canadian stations. They can listen to United States stations at Seattle, San Francisco, Portland and the south, usually in the evening. Rarely can we get Canadian stations. We can never hear them properly, or get a complete program.
There is tremendous production right within the area I am speaking about that does not receive radio reception at the present time. Just last year in the Arrow lakes area alone 100 million feet of lumber were cut. That is a great contribution to the production of this country and to the taxes of this government. In the area I am speaking of, the Kootenay lake area, 50 million feet of lumber were cut. There is a tremendous mineral production in the area concerned. I have not the figures, but they are included in the total area. In the Kootenay West area there is extensive agricultural production, particularly in fruit, dairying and poultry, and there is an extensive tourist trade.
While millions have been spent in developing the C.B.C. in other directions, the people I am speaking about, and I know some other groups in Canada, have been completely denied the opportunity of enjoying the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's radio facilities. At the present time, and until this situation is remedied, the people of whom I am speaking will be forced to obtain their news, their entertainment, their commentaries and programs they wish to enjoy, from United States stations.
Request for Election and Senate Reform
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do urge that the government give consideration to circumstances such as these and by the installation of the low-power relay stations that are necessary for these Canadians, good Canadians, largely living under pioneer conditions, to enjoy the Canadian radio programs and the benefits that the great majority of Canadians have enjoyed for over 30 years.
May I adjourn the debate?

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me, because of the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition, and because of the material he introduced, the debate tonight should rightly centre around the pipe-line bill and the other question of reform of the other place.
I am wondering what will be the position of those hon. members who are sympathetic to questions such as those raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell), if they are expected, as is usual, to support the government on a want of confidence vote.
The Social Credit party do not appear to be in such a peculiar position with respect to this omnibus motion. They have indicated they do not feel that recent actions should require the government to go to the country, yet they may be sympathetic with some of the questions that were raised this afternoon. It is for that reason that I feel the debate has ranged somewhat too far and too wide. Tomorrow, when I take my place in the house again, I expect to continue this debate. I intend to discuss the matter raised by the Leader of the Opposition, and to show that if the rules of this house were broken during the pipe-line debate they were broken by members of the official opposition and by members of the C.C.F. party, not by any members on this side of the house. I hope I shall be allowed to continue in that vein, Mr. Speaker, as it will simply be answering what hon. members on the opposition side of the house said this afternoon.
On Friday last the Leader of the Opposition reiterated a speech he made on an earlier occasion, and I hope I shall be permitted to say that the opposition have been the ones who have broken the rules thus far in this session. May I adjourn the debate?
The hon. member's time is not up.

subtopic: POSTAL SERVICE, MARYSVILLE, N. B.
POSTAL SERVICE, MARYSVILLE, N. B.
speechtext:
What action, if any, has been taken to establish door to door mail delivery at Marysville, New Brunswick?
Answer by: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Postmaster General):
A survey has been carried out by field officers and instructions have been issued to provide letter carrier delivery service as soon as the usual conditions respecting letter slots, house numbers, etc., have been complied with.

subtopic: C. N. R. APPROPRIATIONS, EDMUNDSTON, N. B.
C. N. R. APPROPRIATIONS, EDMUNDSTON, N. B.
speechtext:
1. Has an appropriation been made for a new Canadian National railway station and/or freight terminal at Edmundston, New Brunswick?
Questions
2. What action, if any, is being taken to build a new station and/or freight shed at Edmundston, New Brunswick?
Answer by:	Mr. Langlois, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Transport:
The Canadian National Railways advise as follows:
1.	No appropriation is included in the 1956 capital budget for the construction of a new station. Provision is made in the 1956 budget for the construction of five storage tracks and other track changes. This work is a continuation of extension and alterations commenced in 1954 and continued during 1955.
2.	Plans have been prepared and are now being completed with a view to commencing construction of a new station and freight shed during 1957 if funds are authorized in that year's capital budget.
